enrichment.short_title: Zimbabwe asylum appeal on persecution threshold
key_facts: A Zimbabwean Shona cultural artist appealed after the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissed his asylum appeal against an adjudicator's refusal.
The appellant had been assaulted by Zanu-PF youths after performing at MDC rallies but had not been arrested or detained in Zimbabwe.
The adjudicator found him credible and accepted a well-founded fear of ill treatment, but held past violence did not amount to persecution.
The tribunal misread the adjudicator as having failed to assess future risk and failed to distinguish ill treatment from persecution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision dismissing an asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the adjudicator's finding that past ill treatment fell short of persecution was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator may properly distinguish ill treatment from persecution where a single beating was not particularly vicious and future risk was assessed; the tribunal erred by misinterpreting the adjudicator's reasoning and substituting its own view without first finding the adjudicator wrong.
legal_issues: Whether past assaults by political opponents amounted to persecution
Whether the adjudicator adequately considered future risk of ill treatment
Whether the tribunal correctly applied Demirkaya and Ravichandran on the persecution threshold
Whether the internal flight alternative was available
linked_authorities: Ravichandran v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1996] Imm AR 97
Demirkaya v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1999] IAR 498
Hovarth [2000] Imm AR 552

notes: Commercial stay and solicitor authority application; Donsland analysis and Polish law issues are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Stay refused in shareholders' dispute over solicitor authority
key_facts: ZP and Euroafrica disputed Events of Default under a 1996 Shareholders' Agreement governing a Polonia Lines joint venture.
ZP applied to stay conjoined English proceedings pending Polish proceedings on whether Euroafrica's boards were validly constituted after disputed 2002 EGMs.
Richards Butler had been retained on a general basis through Polish lawyers before the alleged constitutional defects arose.
A July 2004 trial was fixed and substantial preparation had already been undertaken.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in the Commercial Court for a stay of English proceedings pending determination of related Polish proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; Richards Butler had continuing authority to act and a stay would prejudice both parties without realistic risk of re-litigation.
enrichment.ratio: Under Donsland, a solicitor retained on a general litigation retainer retains authority to conduct proceedings even if later unable easily to obtain instructions from a disputed management board; where Polish constitutional issues do not affect the central contractual issues, a stay pending Polish proceedings is unnecessary.
legal_issues: Whether Euroafrica's solicitors had authority to conduct the English proceedings
Whether proceedings should be stayed pending Polish court determination of board validity
Effect of Polish company law on shareholder resolutions and board composition
Whether a judgment obtained by authorised solicitors would bind Euroafrica regardless of later Polish findings
linked_authorities: Donsland Ltd v Van Hoogstraten [2002] EWCA Civ 253
Underwood Son & Piper v Lewis [1894] 2 QB 306

notes: Operation Puma informant nondisclosure appeal; Crown concession and quashing of convictions are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Operation Puma convictions quashed for informant nondisclosure
key_facts: Ghuman, Prior, Parmenter and Bamidele were convicted of conspiracy to cheat the public revenue in a bonded warehouse diversion fraud exceeding £25 million.
After conviction it emerged that London City Bond directors Alfred and Edward Allington were participating informants known to Customs and Excise.
Judge Focke was not told of their informant status at a PII hearing and Alfred Allington gave misleading or dishonest evidence.
Customs officer Bernie Small failed to keep proper informant records and AAD exhibit continuity was compromised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal and late applications for leave to appeal against conviction, including a CCRC reference in Ghuman's case.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted to Prior, Parmenter and Bamidele; all four appellants' convictions quashed, including Bamidele who had pleaded guilty without proper disclosure.
enrichment.ratio: Inadequate disclosure of participating informants, dishonest prosecution evidence at PII hearings, and broken exhibit continuity can taint a prosecution beyond redemption; defendants who pleaded guilty without adequate disclosure should not be in a worse position than those who contested trial.
legal_issues: Whether nondisclosure of participating informants undermined the convictions
Whether an abuse of process application would likely have succeeded with full disclosure
Whether a guilty plea entered without adequate disclosure should stand
Effect of Alfred Allington's dishonest evidence on the safety of convictions

Early & Ors [2003] 1 Cr App R 288

notes: Section 41 sexual history ruling and R v A distinction are comprehensively analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Rape appeal: prostitution evidence excluded under section 41

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: The appellant was convicted by a 10-2 majority of rape after a night of drinking and cannabis at the complainant's flat.
The complainant had worked as a prostitute and the defence sought to cross-examine her about past and contemporaneous prostitution.
The trial judge refused leave under section 41 but permitted limited questioning about payment expectations on the night.
The defence argued exclusion rendered the conviction unsafe and that R v A required a wider reading of section 41.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge, adjourned for argument on R v A.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction safe and cross-examination about prostitution was properly excluded.
enrichment.ratio: General evidence that a complainant was or had been a prostitute does not satisfy section 41(6)'s requirement of specific instances with probative force; R v A does not support reading down section 41 to admit sexual behaviour with third parties where ordinary construction excludes it.
legal_issues: Whether cross-examination about prostitution was admissible under section 41(3)
Whether section 41(6) required specific instances of sexual behaviour
Whether exclusion rendered the jury's verdict on consent unsafe
Whether R v A required section 41 to be read compatibly with article 6 for third-party sexual history
index_terms: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999
linked_authorities: R v Seaboyer
R v Holmes (1871) LR 1 CCR 334

notes: Extended sentence and section 28 disqualification construction clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Extended sentence and section 28 disqualification upheld

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to indecent assault on a 14-year-old girl met online and to possession of category 1 indecent pseudo-photographs.
He received a six-month custodial term with an 18-month extension period under section 85 and a section 28 disqualification from working with children.
A pre-sentence report assessed medium risk of reoffending and noted lack of insight and refusal to undertake a sex offender programme.
On release, probation imposed a licence condition preventing residence with his own children.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal sentence appeal limited to the extension period and the section 28 disqualification order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 28 order was lawful and the 18-month extension was not manifestly excessive, though registration should be for 10 not 7 years.
enrichment.ratio: For section 28 purposes an extended sentence's qualifying term includes the extension period because a custodial sentence under section 76 comprises both custody and licence; Graham S was decided per incuriam on this point.
legal_issues: Whether an extended sentence with a custodial term under 12 months is a qualifying sentence for section 28
Whether the 18-month extension period was manifestly excessive
Construction of custodial sentence for extended sentences under section 85
Effect of probation licence conditions on the appeal
linked_authorities: R v Graham S [2001] 1 Cr App R(S) 335
R v Oliver [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 15

notes: Workplace steps negligence appeal; foreseeability and regulation 12 analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Employer not liable for missing handrail on factory steps
key_facts: Mr Coates tripped on four shallow factory steps used by about 100 employees daily and seriously injured his arm.
The trial judge found Jaguar negligent for failing to provide a handrail and apportioned 25% contributory negligence.
The steps were in good condition, unusually deep, and had been used without incident for years before the accident.
A handrail was installed after the accident on the safety officer's recommendation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal and claimant's cross appeal from Birmingham County Court judgment on negligence and statutory duty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed with costs; claim dismissed and the judge's order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Foreseeability of a trip on ordinary workplace steps does not automatically impose a duty to install a handrail; regulation 5 concerns maintenance rather than provision, and regulation 12(5) did not apply because the steps were not a staircase.
legal_issues: Whether failure to provide a handrail was negligent
Whether regulation 12(5) required handrails on the steps
Whether regulation 5 imposed an absolute duty to provide a handrail
Whether the claimant contributed to the accident

notes: Detailed assessment on CFA Regulation 3(2)(c) and Hollins materiality test; decision complete on enforceability.

enrichment.short_title: CFA held enforceable despite Regulation 3(2)(c) breach
key_facts: Rachid Ghannouchi sued Al Arab over allegations linking An Nahda to Al Qaeda and obtained a £61,000 jury verdict after the defendants withdrew justification.
Carter-Ruck acted under a 100% success fee CFA and billed over £1.3 million including substantial Arabic translation costs.
The defendants challenged CFA validity under Regulations 3(2)(c) and 4 at detailed assessment.
The Costs Judge found the CFA breached Regulation 3(2)(c) but that the breach was not materially adverse under Hollins v Russell.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment of costs following a defamation trial and liability judgment.
enrichment.outcome: CFA enforceable; although Regulation 3(2)(c) was breached, the departure had no materially adverse effect on client protection or administration of justice.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 3(2)(c) on settlement of costs limits recovery of both base costs and success fee unless the court orders otherwise, distinct from Regulation 3(2)(b) on assessment; under Hollins, immaterial regulatory departures do not render a CFA unenforceable, judged at detailed assessment stage.
legal_issues: Construction of Regulation 3(2)(c) on agreed costs reductions
Whether the CFA complied with Regulation 4 explanation requirements
Whether breach of the Regulations rendered the CFA unenforceable
Application of the Hollins v Russell materiality test
linked_authorities: Hollins v Russell
R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State for Health [2003] 2 WLR 692
Awwad v Geraghty

enrichment.short_title: GMC erasure upheld for doctor's sexual misconduct with patient
key_facts: Dr Wentzel, a psychiatric SHO, formed an improper emotional and later sexual relationship with vulnerable patient Ms X.
The GMC found he had sexual intercourse with her in January 1999 and lied to superiors that the relationship was platonic.
After transfer to Taunton he resumed the relationship despite instructions not to contact Ms X.
The GMC erased his name from the register for serious professional misconduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of rehearing under section 40 of the Medical Act 1983 against GMC liability and sanction decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; findings on sexual intercourse in January 1999 and erasure were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: The GMC was entitled to accept Ms X's evidence on the January 1999 intercourse corroborated by surrounding conduct; maintaining public confidence in the profession is paramount and may require erasure even for an otherwise competent doctor with no risk of repetition.
legal_issues: Whether Ms X was a credible witness on the disputed January 1999 intercourse
Whether erasure was disproportionate given Dr Wentzel's abilities and lack of repetition risk
Whether the GMC properly found lack of insight
Balancing public confidence against the doctor's and health service interests

Bijl v GMC [2002] Lloyds Med Rep 60

notes: Share pre-emption and register rectification issues coherently resolved with Hunter and Tett analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Register rectified after breach of share pre-emption articles
key_facts: Mrs Cottrell was registered as holder of 75% of shares after her husband Mervyn Cottrell died without pre-emption procedures being followed.
Mr King, the 25% shareholder, later relied on article 12 pre-emption rights and sought rectification of the register.
Mr King said he was unaware of the pre-emption provisions until late 2001; Mrs Cottrell argued waiver and section 35A protection.
The court found Mr King's pre-emption right became an equitable option when Mrs Cottrell gave notice to the company.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations of ownership with counterclaim for rectification of the company register.
enrichment.outcome: Order for rectification of the register; Mrs Cottrell took shares subject to Mr King's equitable pre-emption interest and waiver was not established.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to comply with pre-emption articles converts a shareholder's right into an equitable option prior to registration; a transferee who is not a purchaser for value takes legal title subject to that equity, and section 35A does not defeat a shareholder's pre-emption equity.
legal_issues: Effect of non-compliance with article 12 pre-emption provisions
Whether Mrs Cottrell was protected by section 35A as a person dealing in good faith
Whether Mr King waived his pre-emption rights
Whether rectification under section 359 was appropriate

Tett v Phoenix Property and Investments Co Ltd [1984] BCLC 599
Smith v Henniker-Major & Co [2003] Ch 182
EIC Services Ltd v Phipps [2003] EWHC 1507 (Ch)

notes: Soliciting murder appeal on self-defence summing-up; court found conviction safe despite absent tailored direction.

key_facts: Sheikh El-Faisal distributed audio tapes urging Muslims to kill non-believers, Jews, Americans and Hindus.
He was convicted of soliciting murder on three counts and racial hatred offences, receiving seven years on the murder counts.
The defence said his references to killing were limited to battlefield self-defence against oppressors of Muslims.
The prosecution case was that the tapes solicited indiscriminate unlawful killing regardless of immediate attack.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against conviction, limited to whether the judge adequately directed the jury on lawful self-defence in soliciting murder.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed; conviction safe despite absence of a more tailored self-defence direction.
enrichment.ratio: Soliciting murder requires the killing encouraged to be unlawful; while a specific direction on battlefield-limited self-defence would have been better, the judge's conventional direction was not erroneous and the jury must have rejected the appellant's limited-intent explanation.
legal_issues: Whether the judge adequately directed the jury on lawful justification for killing solicited
Whether the appellant's battlefield limitation raised a defence to soliciting murder
Whether the prosecution proved solicitation of unlawful rather than self-defensive killing
Safety of conviction where no tailored self-defence direction was requested at trial
linked_authorities: R v Most (1881) 7 QBD 244
